subject: medicine
title: Snake bite: immobilise, reassure, antivenom for systemic or severe local signs

steps.tx: Most snake bites do **not** need antivenom. First aid is reassurance, **immobilisation** of the bitten limb at heart level, removal of rings, and rapid transport (WHO South-East Asia snakebite guideline). Do not apply tourniquets, cut, suck or apply herbs; they worsen injury. Record bite time, snake description if safe, and evolving swelling.
steps.say: Most snake bites do not need antivenom. First aid is reassurance, immobilisation of the bitten limb at heart level, removal of rings, and rapid transport. Do not apply tourniquets, cut, suck or apply herbs. Record bite time and evolving swelling.

steps.tx: The photo shows correct snakebite first aid inside an ambulance. The bitten forearm rests on a rigid splint and is carried in a sling at **heart level**, keeping the limb still during rapid transport to care. A paramedic supervises the transfer. The crossed out symbols stress what to avoid: never apply a **tourniquet**, and never cut or suck the wound, since these actions worsen injury. Reassurance plus **immobilisation** and fast transfer matter more than any local intervention.
steps.say: This photo shows correct snakebite first aid. The bitten forearm is immobilised on a rigid splint and supported in a sling at heart level while a paramedic arranges rapid transport. The warning symbol reminds you never to apply a tourniquet and never to cut or suck the wound, because those actions worsen injury. Reassure the patient, keep the limb still, remove rings, and transfer quickly for assessment for antivenom.

steps.tx: Give **antivenom** only for systemic envenoming (spontaneous bleeding, incoagulable blood, neurotoxicity, shock, kidney injury) or severe local envenoming (rapidly progressive swelling). Test clotting with the 20-minute whole blood clotting test where labs are limited. Have adrenaline ready: antivenom reactions are treated by pausing the infusion and giving intramuscular adrenaline.
steps.say: Give antivenom only for systemic envenoming or severe local envenoming. Test clotting with the 20-minute whole blood clotting test where labs are limited. Have adrenaline ready, because antivenom reactions are treated by pausing the infusion and giving intramuscular adrenaline.

steps.tx: Neurotoxic bites cause descending paralysis: ptosis first, then breathing failure. Support the airway and ventilation; **antivenom** works best early. Haemotoxic bites cause bleeding and kidney injury, so monitor urine, clotting and renal function. Antibiotics and tetanus cover are secondary; pressure immobilisation is for neurotoxic elapid bites where taught.
steps.say: Neurotoxic bites cause descending paralysis, ptosis first, then breathing failure. Support airway and ventilation. Haemotoxic bites cause bleeding and kidney injury, so monitor urine, clotting and renal function.

steps.tx: After antivenom, keep watching the limb and the clotting. Mark the swelling edge and repeat the **20-minute clotting test**, because coagulopathy can return as venom depots empty. Most tense swelling is venom oedema, not compartment syndrome, so fasciotomy needs measured pressures and senior agreement, not a tight look alone. Days later, fever with rash and joint pain means **serum sickness**; it follows antivenom and needs medical review, not another dose at home.
steps.say: Recheck the swelling edge and the clotting after antivenom, because both can worsen again. A tense limb is usually venom swelling rather than compartment syndrome, so surgery needs measured pressures and a senior decision. Fever with rash and joint pain days later is serum sickness, and the patient should come back for review.
